text:
No study located directly validates inference-time deletion/shuffling sensitivity as a predictor of gains from subsequent model changes. Related evidence supports narrower conclusions: [Woolridge et al. (2021)](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2955/paper8.pdf) found SASRec relatively robust to history shuffling and highlighted ambiguous timestamps; this tests dependence on ordering, not whether increasing sensitivity improves generalization. [Petrov et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833) found recency-weighted pairwise models competitive with Transformers across several benchmarks, showing that useful history information need not require higher-order interactions. Neither establishes a diagnostic-to-improvement relationship or transfers directly to HSTU on these four categories.

Methodological inference: training positive–negative margin changes measure sensitivity on observed training targets and sampled competitors; memorization and score-scale changes can inflate them without improving ranks. Paired held-out target-rank changes, keeping each user’s target and candidate set fixed across perturbations, more directly measure ranking dependence. Still, degradation after deletion/shuffling shows reliance under corrupted inputs, not that retraining with a proposed change will help. Deletion also changes history length/recency; shuffling can create out-of-distribution histories. [Krichene and Rendle (2020)](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) demonstrate that sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons; fixed 99-negative candidates support the pinned benchmark comparison, not full-catalog conclusions.

Repeated histories, overlapping prefixes, and multiple perturbations of one user are dependent observations: aggregate paired effects per user and bootstrap users. Repeatedly choosing changes from diagnostic and validation feedback risks adaptive overfitting, as illustrated by [Dwork et al. (2015)](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper/2015/hash/bad5f33780c42f2588878a9d07405083-Abstract.html). Treat sensitivity as hypothesis generation, with no defensible numerical uplift forecast; prioritize controlled, single-model HSTU ablations of loss, sampling, regularization, and recency treatment, selected by the fixed macro validation HR@10.
